summary: A best current practice describing what the Internet community expects from Computer Security Incident Response Teams. It cannot define requirements right for every team, but it lists topics each team should state clearly, like its mission and services.

plainLanguage.summary: A computer security incident response team is the group that handles security incidents for a defined set of users or sites. RFC 2350 says what such a team should publish so that its community knows what to expect: who it serves, what it will and will not do, how to report an incident, and how the information it handles is treated.

questions: what to expect from a csirt
computer security incident response team guidelines
what should a csirt publish about itself
what is the csirt template in rfc 2350
how do csirt teams cooperate with each other
subtitle: What the Internet community should be able to find out about the incident response team it relies on.

tldr.problem: Users and sites that rely on an incident response team do not know in advance what it will do for them, how to reach it, or what it will say about them, which leads to misunderstandings during an incident.
tldr.mechanism: The document lists the topics every response team should publish, in the form of a template a team completes and signs, covering its charter, policies, services, reporting forms and disclaimers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2350 is BCP 21 and is not obsoleted. It sets no single policy: it tells teams what to state and leaves the answers to each team.

today: RFC 2350 is a Best Current Practice document, BCP 21, and is neither obsoleted nor updated by any RFC listed for it. It describes expectations rather than a protocol, so it stays in force as guidance for teams that publish a description of themselves.

sections.title: What the Community Should Expect of a CSIRT
sections.content:
For the purposes of this document, a Computer Security Incident Response Team (CSIRT) is a team that performs, coordinates and supports the response to security incidents that involve sites within a defined constituency. Any group calling itself a CSIRT for a specific constituency must react to reported security incidents, and to threats to that constituency, in ways which the specific community agrees to be in its general interest.

To be considered a CSIRT, a team must provide a secure channel for receiving reports about suspected incidents, provide assistance to members of its constituency in handling these incidents, and disseminate incident-related information to its constituency and to other involved parties. The document is not referring to police or other law enforcement bodies which may investigate computer-related crime: CSIRT members need not have any powers beyond those of ordinary citizens.

The goal of the document is to provide a framework for presenting the important subjects related to incident response that are of concern to the community. It cannot define a set of requirements appropriate for all teams, and it makes no attempt to specify the correct answer to any one topic area; each topic is discussed in terms of what that topic means. Details of a CSIRT change with time, so the document also insists that a completed template carry the date of its last update and say how to find out about future updates, since outdated documents can do more harm than good. Without active participation from users, the effectiveness of the CSIRT's services can be greatly diminished, and reporting is the part where users most need to know what to do and where to send it.
sections.plainLanguage: A response team is the group you call when something has been compromised. This document does not tell you how to run one or what it should promise. It tells you which questions every team should answer in writing, so you can find the answers before you need them, and so the team cannot surprise you later.

sections.title: Publishing Policies, Procedures and Contact Details
sections.content:
Each user who has access to a CSIRT should know as much as possible about the services of and interactions with that team long before they are actually needed. A clear statement of the policies and procedures of a CSIRT helps the constituent understand how best to report incidents and what support to expect afterwards. Clear expectations, particularly of the limitations of the services provided by a CSIRT, make interaction with it more efficient and effective.

There are different kinds of response teams: some have very broad constituencies, some have more bounded ones, and still others have very restricted ones. Regardless of the type, the constituency supported by the team must know the team's policies and procedures, so it is mandatory that response teams publish such information. Not all policies need to be publicly available: understanding the internal operation of a team is not necessary in order to interact with it, as when reporting an incident or receiving guidance on how to analyse or secure one's systems.

The document recommends that each CSIRT publish its guidelines and procedures on its own information server, so that constituents can easily access them, and notes that it would be very useful to have a central repository containing all the completed CSIRT templates, although none exists at the time of writing. Regardless of the source from which the information is retrieved, the user of the template must check its authenticity, and it is highly recommended that such vital documents be protected by digital signatures, so that the user can verify that the template was indeed published by the CSIRT and has not been tampered with.

The template should also carry the date of its last update, a distribution list for notifications, the location where the document can be found, and full contact information: the name of the team, mailing address, time zone, telephone and facsimile numbers, other telecommunication, electronic mail address, public keys and encryption information, team members, operating hours and holiday schedule, and any additional contact points for specific services.
sections.plainLanguage: The team must publish what it does and how to reach it, and the publication has to be dated, because a team changes over time and an old document misleads. The document should carry a digital signature, so a reader can check that it really came from the team and was not altered on the way.

sections.title: Working with Other Response Teams
sections.content:
Many computer security incidents originate outside local community boundaries and affect inside sites, and others originate inside the local community and affect hosts or users on the outside. Handling them will therefore involve multiple sites and potentially multiple CSIRTs, and resolving them requires cooperation between individual sites and CSIRTs, and between CSIRTs. Inter-CSIRT interactions can include asking other teams for advice, disseminating knowledge of problems, and working cooperatively to resolve a security incident affecting one or more of the constituencies.

Constituent communities need to know exactly how their CSIRT will be working with other CSIRTs and with organizations outside their constituency, and what information will be shared, because very sensitive information about individual constituents may be disclosed in the process.

In establishing relationships to support such interactions, CSIRTs must decide what kinds of agreements can exist between them so as to share yet safeguard information, whether the relationship can be disclosed, and if so to whom. The document notes the difference between a peering agreement, where the CSIRTs involved agree to work together and share information, and simple co-operation, where a CSIRT simply contacts another CSIRT and asks for help or advice. The details of that process are up to the teams involved and are beyond the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Most incidents cross boundaries, so the team will be talking to other teams, to vendors, to police or to the press. The published policy should say what kinds of contact exist, what information can travel, and whether a formal agreement exists with the other team or it is only an informal request for help.

sections.title: Establishing Secure Communications
sections.content:
Once one party has decided to share information with another, all parties involved need secure communications channels. Here secure refers to the protected transmission of information shared between different parties, and not to the appropriate use of the information by the parties. The goals of secure communication are confidentiality, meaning that somebody else cannot access the content; integrity, meaning that somebody else cannot manipulate the content; and authenticity, meaning that the receiver knows whether they are communicating with the right person.

It is very easy to send forged e-mail, and not hard to establish a false identity by telephone. Cryptographic techniques such as Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) or Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) can provide effective ways of securing e-mail, and with the correct equipment it is also possible to secure telephone communication. But before using such mechanisms, both parties need the right infrastructure, which means preparation in advance. The most important preparation is ensuring the authenticity of the cryptographic keys used in secure communication. Public keys, as used by techniques like PGP and PEM, must be authenticated before use: PGP relies on a web of trust where users sign the keys of other users, while PEM relies on a hierarchy where certification authorities sign the keys of users. Secret keys must be exchanged before the communication over a secure channel, because both sender and receiver must know them.

The document is not about the technical and administrative problems of secure communications. The point is that response teams must support and use a method to secure the communications between themselves and their constituents, and the level of protection it provides must be acceptable to the constituent community.
sections.plainLanguage: Incident reports travel between organizations, so the channel has to protect the content, show that nobody altered it, and prove who is talking. The key step happens before the incident: exchanging and authenticating the keys used for encryption, so that both sides are ready when the phone rings.

sections.title: The Charter of a Response Team
sections.content:
Every CSIRT must have a charter which specifies what it is to do and the authority under which it will do it. The charter should include at least a mission statement, the constituency, the sponsorship or affiliation, and the authority.

The mission statement should focus on the team's core activities. To be considered a CSIRT, the team must support the reporting of incidents and support its constituency by dealing with incidents, and the goals and purposes of a team require clear, unambiguous definition.

A CSIRT's constituency can be determined in several ways: it could be a company's employees or its paid subscribers, or it could be defined in terms of a technological focus such as the users of a particular operating system. The definition of the constituency should create a perimeter around the group to whom the team provides service, and the policy section should explain how requests from outside that perimeter will be handled. If a CSIRT decides not to disclose its constituency, it should explain the reasoning: for-fee CSIRTs will not list their clients but will declare that they provide a service to a large group of customers kept confidential because of the clients' contracts. Constituencies might overlap, as when an ISP provides a CSIRT which delivers services to customer sites that also have CSIRTs.

The sponsoring organization, which authorizes the actions of the CSIRT, helps users understand the background and set-up of the team, and is vital information for building trust. The authority section varies greatly: an organizational CSIRT is given its authority by the management of the organization, while a community CSIRT is supported and chosen by the community, usually in an advisory role. A CSIRT may or may not have the authority to intervene in the operation of all the systems within its perimeter, and should identify the scope of its control as distinct from the perimeter of its constituency. Disclosure of a team's authority may expose it to claims of liability, and every team should seek legal advice on these matters.
sections.plainLanguage: The charter answers four questions: what the team is for, who it serves, who authorizes it, and what power it has. The team should also state where its authority stops, because a team that says it can take over a machine has to say so in writing.

sections.title: Policies: Support Levels and Disclosure of Information
sections.content:
It is critical that incident response teams define their policies. The types of incident the team is able to address, and the level of support it will offer for each type, should be summarized in list form. The level of support may change depending on factors such as the team's workload and the completeness of the information available, and those factors should be outlined with their impact explained. Because any list of known incident types will be incomplete with regard to possible or future incidents, the team should also give some background on the default support for incident types not otherwise mentioned.

The reporting and disclosure policy should make clear who will be the recipients of a report in each circumstance, and should note whether the team will operate through another CSIRT or directly with a member of another constituency. The document lists the related groups a CSIRT will interact with: incident response teams, vendors, law-enforcement agencies, the press, and others such as research activities. Cooperation between CSIRTs can be facilitated by the use of unique ticket number assignment combined with explicit handoff procedures, which reduces misunderstandings and duplicated effort, assists in incident tracking and prevents loops in communication.

The default status of any and all security-related information a team receives will usually be confidential, but rigid adherence to this makes the team appear to be an informational black hole, which may reduce the likelihood of obtaining cooperation from clients and other organizations. The template should define what information the team will report or disclose, to whom, and when. Different teams are likely to be subject to different legal restraints requiring or limiting disclosure, especially if they work in different jurisdictions, and may have reporting requirements imposed by their sponsoring organization; each template should specify any such constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: The policy section says which incidents the team handles, how much help it gives, and what factors change that, including what to do about incident types the list does not mention. It also says what information leaves the team, to whom, and under what rules, since keeping everything secret by default stops people from ever reporting anything.

sections.title: Services: Triage, Coordination, Resolution and Prevention
sections.content:
Services provided by a CSIRT fall into two categories: real-time activities directly related to incident response, and non-real-time proactive activities that support it. The second category, and part of the first, consist of services that are optional in the sense that not all CSIRTs will offer them.

Incident response usually includes assessing incoming reports about incidents, which is incident triage, and following up with other CSIRTs, ISPs and sites, which is incident coordination. Triage includes report assessment, meaning the interpretation of incoming incident reports, prioritizing them and relating them to ongoing incidents and trends, and verification, meaning help in determining whether an incident has really occurred and its scope. Coordination includes information categorization, meaning categorizing the incident-related information such as logfiles and contact information with respect to the disclosure policy, and coordination itself, meaning notification of other involved parties on a need-to-know basis. A third range of services, incident resolution, helps a local site recover from an incident and is typically optional: technical assistance, which may include analysis of compromised systems; eradication, meaning elimination of the cause of the incident and its effects; and recovery, meaning aid in restoring affected systems and services to their status before the incident.

Proactive services may include information provision, such as an archive of known vulnerabilities, patches or resolutions of past problems, or advisory mailing lists; security tools for auditing a site's security; education and training; product evaluation; and site security auditing and consulting.

The use of reporting forms makes it simpler for both users and teams to deal with incidents. The constituent can prepare answers to important questions before contacting the team, and the team gets all the necessary information at once with the first report. It is most efficient to provide the forms through the online information services of the team, with pointers in the description document, statements about appropriate use, and guidelines for when and how to use them. A disclaimer at the end of the template is recommended, because although the document does not constitute a contract, liability may conceivably result from its descriptions of services and purposes, and each CSIRT should check the disclaimer with a lawyer.
sections.plainLanguage: The services section describes the path of an incident: a report arrives and is assessed and checked, the people who need to know are told, and then help is given to clean up and restore the affected system. Reporting forms let the person who discovered the problem answer the obvious questions in advance, so the first report is complete.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document discusses the operation of Computer Security Incident Response Teams and their interactions with their constituencies and with other organizations. It is therefore not directly concerned with the security of protocols, applications or network systems themselves, and it is not even concerned with particular responses and reactions to security incidents, but only with the appropriate description of the responses provided by CSIRTs.

Nonetheless, it is vital that the CSIRTs themselves operate securely. That means they must establish secure communication channels with other teams and with members of their constituency, and they must secure their own systems and infrastructure, to protect the interests of their constituency and to maintain the confidentiality of the identity of victims and reporters of security incidents.
sections.plainLanguage: The document is not about securing protocols, but a response team that cannot keep its own systems and its own communications safe is a poor guardian for the people who report to it.

viz.caption: THE TEMPLATE OUTLINE FROM APPENDIX D OF RFC 2350
THE SERVICES A RESPONSE TEAM MAY OFFER

items.title: Incident triage
items.text: Report assessment and verification: interpret and prioritize incoming reports, and check whether an incident really occurred.

items.title: Incident coordination
items.text: Information categorization and coordination: sort the information by disclosure policy and notify the parties who need to know.

items.title: Incident resolution
items.text: Technical assistance, eradication and recovery: analyse, clean up and restore the affected systems.

items.title: Proactive activities
items.text: Information provision, security tools, education and training, product evaluation, and site security auditing.
